teach.note: Show the camera plan as a cycle: wide, middle, detail, wide again. Say that moving through the scene gives structure. Ask pupils to place senses at each stage.

teach.heading: Worked model: a descriptive paragraph

model.problem: Write a description suggested by this picture of an empty seaside pier in winter.
steps: Open with a wide shot using a metaphor for the sea.
Add the senses: sound of wind, taste of salt, touch of cold railing.
Move to the detail: one lamp, one gull.
Vary sentence length: a short sentence for impact.
Close by echoing the opening image.
model.answer: The sea heaved like a sleeping animal under a sky the colour of old pewter. Wind combed the pier, whistling through the gaps in the weathered boards, and each railing was so cold that it seemed to bite back. The arcade stood shuttered, its painted lights dead. Salt stung the tongue. At the far end, a single lamp glowed, a small, stubborn yellow. A gull perched beneath it, motionless. Nothing else moved. Beyond the lamp, the grey sea breathed in and out, patient, unhurried, as if waiting for the summer to return.

teach.note: Read the model; pupils tick the techniques: personification, simile, senses, short sentence, repeated sound (sibilance). Say the paragraph is 95 words, ideal for a timed task, and it does not tell the reader to feel lonely; it shows with details.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence is the strongest description?
options: The pier was very lonely and sad.
A single lamp glowed, a small, stubborn yellow, above a motionless gull.
The pier was big, grey, cold, old and empty.
check.why: B shows loneliness through specific details and controlled rhythm. A tells; C piles up adjectives without a unifying effect.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is telling; C is a list of adjectives with no effect.

teach.heading: Sentence and punctuation variety
bullets: Short sentence for impact: Nothing else moved.
Complex sentence with participle: Wind combed the pier, whistling ...
Use a semi-colon between linked ideas.
Check commas, capitals and spelling in the last five minutes.
teach.note: Say AO6 is worth 16 marks: show semi-colons, dashes, short sentences. Warn about comma splices. EAL support: sentence stems.

practice: Write an opening sentence using a metaphor for the sea.
Add one sentence with two senses (not sight).
Rewrite 'The sky was grey' using a simile or personification.
independent: Core: Write the first paragraph of a description for the pier prompt (80 words).
Extend: Write three paragraphs that move from wide to detail to wide, using at least three senses.
Stretch: Write a 300-word description with a deliberate shift in tone and a final echo of the opening.
exit: Name two ways to give a description structure.
Rewrite 'It was cold' with a precise image.
Big question: how can I make a reader see without telling them what to feel?
lessons.homework: Describe in 120 words the view from your window at an unusual time of day, using at least three senses and one simile.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a four-box camera planner and a word bank (weathered, shuttered, stubborn, pewter). EAL/international: pre-teach 'pier', 'arcade', 'out of season', 'weathered', 'shuttered'; idiom 'the calm before the storm' = quiet just before trouble; stems: 'In the distance there was ...', 'The air smelled of ...', 'It looked as if ...'. Cultural note: seaside holiday towns and piers, winter closures. Stretch: write in the second person to alter the viewpoint.

lessons.unit: P1-B-Q5: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
lessons.title: Question 5: narrative writing with a controlled structure
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I shape a short story so that it feels complete in 40 minutes?
objectives: Plan a short narrative with one focus and a clear ending
Open and close a story with deliberate effect
Use dialogue, thought and pace to show character rather than explain it
successCriteria: All: write a story with an opening, a problem and an ending
Most: control pace, using sentence length and paragraphs
Some: echo a motif from the beginning at the end to create shape

keywords.def: a story or account of events
an image or idea that is repeated
spoken words between characters
a scene from an earlier time
the way the problem is dealt with at the end

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the four stages of the camera plan from the last lesson.
Write an opening sentence that starts in the middle of an action.
Define 'cliffhanger'.

teach.heading: The task
bullets: Task: a story about a moment of waiting for news.
Choose: one place, one character, one problem.
Write about 450-600 words in 30 minutes.
Plan for five minutes; check for five.
teach.note: Task: 'Write a story about a moment when someone is waiting for news.' (40 marks). Remind pupils that Paper 1 Section B has one task, either descriptive or narrative; pupils choose the one they can do best. Cultural context: in the UK, news may arrive by phone, letter or doorbell; any culture's version is welcome.

teach.heading: A five-point plan

timeline.label: 1. Open
timeline.text: start in the moment, with a precise detail (the motif)

timeline.label: 2. Build
timeline.text: show waiting: time, small actions, thoughts

timeline.label: 3. Twist
timeline.text: a sound, a message or a decision changes things

timeline.label: 4. Climax
timeline.text: the news arrives, in few words

timeline.label: 5. Close
timeline.text: echo the motif; end with a feeling or image

teach.note: Say that short stories do not cover long periods. A tight timeline gives control. Ask pupils to pick an unusual starting point (the news just arrived, or an object on a table). Introduce a motif as the 'thread' to link the opening to the ending.

teach.heading: Worked model: opening and ending

model.problem: Write the opening and the ending of a story about a moment of waiting for news.
steps: Opening: start with a concrete motif, the kettle, and a time.
Show the waiting through small actions rather than saying 'she was nervous'.
Ending: bring back the kettle, but changed by what has happened.
Keep the final sentence short.
model.answer: OPENING: The kettle clicked off for the third time, and still Nadia did not pour. The phone lay face down on the table like a card she was afraid to turn over. ... ENDING: The phone rang. She listened; she said, 'Yes. Yes. Thank you.' Then she lifted the kettle, and for the first time that day her hands were steady.

teach.note: Note that the motif of the kettle returns at the end with a changed meaning. Also note that the opening starts in the moment and the ending is short. Ask: what has changed in the final kettle? Draw out that repetition with a difference gives shape.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which opening is strongest for this task?
options: The kettle clicked off for the third time, and still Nadia did not pour.
Nadia was very nervous and could not wait any longer for the news.
On Monday Nadia woke up, had breakfast, went to school and then waited.
check.why: A begins in the moment with a concrete motif and implies tension. B tells the emotion; C lists a day and loses focus.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A; C tells emotions; B is a list of events rather than a moment.

teach.heading: Dialogue and punctuation

misconception.wrong: "I am waiting" said Nadia, "for the call." She said it nervous.
misconception.right: "I'm waiting for the call," said Nadia, her fingers tight round the mug.

teach.note: Say direct speech needs a new line for each speaker and accurate punctuation. Idiom: 'to be on edge' = to be tense and nervous.

practice: Choose a motif and write your opening sentence.
Write three sentences showing waiting through small actions only.
Write the closing sentence using the same motif with a changed meaning.
independent: Core: Write the opening and ending paragraphs for the task.
Extend: Write the full story in four paragraphs with the five-point plan.
Stretch: Rewrite your story using a flashback in paragraph two and explain the effect.
exit: Name the five stages of the plan.
What is a motif and why is it useful?
Big question: how do I make a short story feel complete?
lessons.homework: Write a 200-word story ending that echoes an object introduced at the opening, then annotate where it returns.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a plan template with five numbered boxes and a bank of 'small actions' (tapping, pacing, checking). EAL/international: pre-teach 'motif', 'kettle', 'steady', 'on edge', 'echo'; idiom 'to hold your breath' = to wait anxiously; stems: 'She could not stop ...', 'The silence seemed ...', 'At last, ...'. Cultural note: a kettle and tea are common in UK homes at stressful moments; use any familiar object. Stretch: write in first person present tense and keep it consistent.

lessons.unit: SC-W: Subject content: writing across the course
lessons.title: Writing for different purposes: explain, instruct, inform, argue
lessons.bigQuestion: How does my purpose change the way I write the same topic?
objectives: Name the writing purposes in the GCSE range: describe, narrate, explain, instruct, inform, argue
Match features of language and structure to each purpose
Adapt one topic for two purposes and two audiences
successCriteria: All: name the purpose of a text
Most: choose features that suit the purpose
Some: rewrite the same content for a new purpose and audience with controlled register
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: instructions and explanations in practical reports
lessons.smsc: Social: communicating respectfully with different audiences

keywords.def: what the writer wants the text to do
the people the text is written for
the level of formality in language
a command verb used for instructions
a question asked for effect, not for an answer

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three things stated before every Paper 2 Question 5 (audience, purpose and ...).
Write a sentence giving an instruction.
Is 'Hey guys, check this out' formal or informal?

teach.heading: Six purposes

head: Purpose
Typical features
Example opening
rows: On the day the letter came ...

teach.note: Say the specification names these six purposes; pupils should be able to write in all. Ask pupils to give a real-world example of each (recipe, news, letter). For EAL pupils, say we still expect Standard English whatever the accent or first language.

teach.heading: Same topic, two purposes

left.title: Inform (for parents)
points: The canteen serves hot meals from 12.00 to 1.00.
Vegetarian and halal options are offered daily.

right.title: Argue (to the headteacher)
points: Surely every pupil deserves a hot lunch that is affordable.
At £2.50, a meal is too expensive for many families.
We must act now to provide free lunches.

teach.note: Show that the topic 'school lunch' can be informing or arguing. Ask pupils to notice register, fact versus opinion and sentence forms. Point out that audience (headteacher or pupils) changes vocabulary too.

teach.heading: Worked model: adapting a paragraph

model.problem: Rewrite this informative sentence for an argument to the headteacher: 'The school library closes at 3.30.'
steps: Identify the facts: the library, the time 3.30.
Add a stance: closing early harms pupils.
Add a persuasive device: a rhetorical question or a triplet.
Adjust register: formal but forceful.
model.answer: Surely a school that values reading should not lock its library at 3.30, just when pupils have time to read, research and revise? Closing early denies the children who need it most a quiet place to learn.

teach.note: Model the rewrite step by step: keep facts, change features. Ask where the register moves from neutral to persuasive. Say that using the same facts in both texts shows that the purpose changes the choices.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence argues rather than informs?
options: First, wash your hands for twenty seconds.
The mosque library holds 2,000 books.
Surely every community deserves a library that is open when people can use it.
check.why: C uses an opinion and a rhetorical question. A is an instruction; B is a neutral fact.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A uses imperatives (instruct); B informs.

teach.heading: Audience and register
bullets: Friend: informal, contractions, humour.
Headteacher: formal, full sentences, polite.
Younger children: simple words, short sentences.
Newspaper readers: clear, engaging, balanced.
teach.note: Say: the same writer changes tone for a friend and for a head teacher. Idiom: 'to strike the right note' = to use the correct tone.

practice: Write one sentence for each of these purposes about a school trip: inform, instruct, argue.
Rewrite 'You must be quiet!' for a polite note to a neighbour.
Choose the purpose for each text: a recipe, a leaflet about flu jabs, a letter to the council.
independent: Core: Write 60 words to inform parents about a school trip, then 60 words to argue for it.
Extend: Rewrite the argument paragraph for pupils aged 8, changing register.
Stretch: Write a 150-word explanation of how a rainbow forms, then describe it in a poetic paragraph; compare your choices.
exit: Name the six purposes.
Which feature is typical of instruction?
Big question: how does purpose change my writing?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word instruction on making tea and a 100-word argument for why everyone should learn to cook; underline three differences.
lessons.send: SEND: give a purpose-feature matching card sort and a sentence frame for each purpose. EAL/international: pre-teach 'purpose', 'audience', 'register', 'imperative'; idioms 'to strike the right note', 'to put it bluntly'; stems: 'First, ...', 'Because ..., therefore ...', 'It is clear that ...'. Cultural note: British letters often open 'Dear Sir or Madam' and close 'Yours faithfully' when the name is unknown; 'Yours sincerely' when it is known. Stretch: write the same paragraph in three registers.

lessons.unit: SC-W: Subject content: writing across the course
lessons.title: Standard English, grammar and punctuation for technical accuracy
lessons.bigQuestion: How can accurate writing add marks without making my writing dull?
objectives: Use Standard English grammar in formal writing
Punctuate complex sentences, avoiding comma splices
Vary sentence structures for effect
successCriteria: All: write in complete sentences with capital letters and full stops
Most: use commas, apostrophes and semi-colons correctly
Some: vary sentence openings and lengths deliberately for effect
lessons.crossCurricular: MFL and Arabic: comparing sentence structures across languages
lessons.smsc: Social: respect for different dialects while using Standard English where needed

keywords.def: the grammar and vocabulary used in formal writing across the UK, not an accent
two main clauses wrongly joined by only a comma
joins two closely linked main clauses
shows possession or missing letters
the verb matches the subject: they were, not they was

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: what is the difference between a main clause and a subordinate clause?
Correct: 'We was late for school'.
Add a full stop and capital letter to: it was raining we stayed in.

teach.heading: Standard English: grammar, not accent
teach.note: Say clearly: Standard English is about grammar and vocabulary, not accent; every accent is welcome. Dialect or non-standard forms may appear in dialogue for effect, but narration and formal writing use Standard English. For international pupils, note that some forms (we was, I done it) are common in speech around the UK but not in exam writing.

teach.heading: Fix the comma splice

left.title: Comma splice (wrong)
points: The sea was calm, the boats stayed in the harbour.
I was tired, I kept writing.

right.title: Fixed (right)
points: The sea was calm; the boats stayed in the harbour.
I was tired, but I kept writing.
I was tired. I kept writing.

teach.note: Show three fixes: full stop, semi-colon, conjunction. Ask pupils to decide which gives the best rhythm. Point out that fixing is easy once you spot two complete sentences.

teach.heading: Worked model: upgrading a paragraph

model.problem: Improve this paragraph for technical accuracy and variety: 'it was dark we walked home. we was cold. the streetlights was flickering the road was wet.'
steps: Fix capitals and full stops.
Correct 'we was' and 'the streetlights was'.
Split or join the comma splice with a semi-colon or conjunction.
Vary the openings and add one short sentence.
model.answer: It was dark when we walked home. We were cold. The streetlights were flickering; the road was wet and shone like black glass. Nobody spoke.

teach.note: Read the draft aloud, then the model. Ask pupils to count the techniques added: variety of openings, a semi-colon, a participle phrase, a short sentence. Emphasise accuracy as well as variety.

teach.heading: Hinge question

options: The rain stopped, we went out.
The rain stopped; we went out.
The rain stopped we went out.
check.why: B uses a semi-colon to join two linked main clauses. A is a comma splice; C has no punctuation at all.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is a splice; C is non-standard.

teach.heading: Apostrophes at a glance

misconception.wrong: The dog wagged it's tail, and the childrens' coats were wet.
misconception.right: The dog wagged its tail, and the children's coats were wet.

teach.note: Run a quick quiz. Remind pupils: its (belonging) versus it's (it is).

practice: Correct five non-standard sentences supplied by the teacher.
Fix three comma splices in three different ways.
Write one sentence with a semi-colon and one with a participle opening.
independent: Core: Edit a 60-word paragraph with ten errors planted by your teacher.
Extend: Rewrite your own earlier paragraph to improve sentence variety and accuracy.
Stretch: Write a 150-word paragraph with at least five different sentence types, all accurately punctuated.
exit: Is Standard English an accent? Explain.
Fix: 'It was late, we went home.'
Big question: how can accuracy add marks without making writing dull?
lessons.homework: Proofread a page of your own writing from this half-term, correct at least ten errors and list your three most common mistakes.
lessons.send: SEND: give a colour-coded proofreading checklist and allow a word processor with spellcheck for drafts. EAL/international: pre-teach 'splice', 'apostrophe', 'agreement'; idioms 'to get your facts straight', 'a slip of the pen'; stems: 'The correct form is ...', 'This is a comma splice because ...'. Cultural note: UK regional dialects are valued; Standard English is a shared formal code. Stretch: study how a published writer uses fragments for effect and imitate it.
